clm-stanford-university-bca-honor-code-f.text: Stanford BCA guidance treats generative AI like assistance from another person when an instructor has not stated a policy. Using AI to substantially complete an assignment or exam is not permitted in that default context. Students should acknowledge non-incidental AI use and disclose when in doubt. Instructors may set course policies.

evidence.quote: Absent a clear statement from a course instructor, use of or consultation with generative AI shall be treated analogously to assistance from another person. In particular, using generative AI tools to substantially complete an assignment or exam (e.g. by entering exam or assignment questions) is not permitted. Students should acknowledge the use of generative AI (other than incidental use) and default to disclosing such assistance when in doubt.
evidence.location: Captured official text line 108; HTML text extraction; raw source retained privately

clm-stanford-university-gsb-ai-policy.text: For Stanford Graduate School of Business (GSB) MBA and MSx courses, instructors may not ban student use of AI tools for take-home coursework, including assignments and exams. Instructors may choose whether to allow AI for in-class work. For PhD and undergraduate courses, GSB follows the university-wide Generative AI Policy Guidance from the Office of Community Standards.

evidence.quote: MBA/MSx courses: Instructors may not ban student use of AI tools for take-home coursework, including assignments and exams. Instructors may choose whether to allow student use of AI tools for in-class work, including exams. Except for in-class exams, students should be allowed to use AI tools in cases where they are able to use the internet and electronic devices. In-class assignments for which electronic devices are prohibited inherently also prohibit use of the internet, AI tools, tablets, laptops, calculators, etc.
evidence.location: Captured official text line 72; HTML text extraction; raw source retained privately

evidence.quote: PhD/Undergraduate courses: Follow the Generative AI Policy Guidance from Stanford’s Office of Community Standards.
evidence.location: Captured official text line 73; HTML text extraction; raw source retained privately

clm-stanford-university-md-ai-policy.text: Stanford School of Medicine MD and MSPA programs have a formal AI policy: students may use AI for learning, clarification, and grammar/style editing unless contrary to assignment instructions. AI use for closed-book exams or assignments where internet is restricted is prohibited unless explicitly authorized by faculty. Students are responsible for all AI-generated content they submit, must disclose and cite substantial AI contributions, and violations may result in disciplinary action.

evidence.quote: Assessments: The use of AI tools is discouraged for any activities in which students are evaluated on their own knowledge or skills, unless explicitly granted permission by the faculty. Unless explicitly advised by individual instructors, the use of AI tools is prohibited for any “closed book” exams or assignments where internet use is restricted.
evidence.location: Captured official text line 122; HTML text extraction; raw source retained privately

evidence.quote: Learning and Clarification: Students may utilize AI to enhance their understanding of medical concepts, definitions, and for grammar/style editing, provided it does not conflict with specific assignment instructions or be inconsistent with faculty-authorized tasks as detailed below.
evidence.location: Captured official text line 111; HTML text extraction; raw source retained privately

evidence.quote: Any substantial contributions from AI tools on assignments, presentations, and scholarly abstracts or proposals must be disclosed and properly cited. This includes the tool name, model/version, date, query, and output excerpt. For example: ChatGPT (GPT-4; June 10, 2025), prompt: “Explain ARDS pathophysiology,” output used in Section 2.
evidence.location: Captured official text line 127; HTML text extraction; raw source retained privately

evidence.quote: AI tools may not be listed as authors on scholarly works.

clm-stanford-university-md-phi-prohibiti.text: Stanford Medicine and UIT strictly prohibit entering Protected Health Information (PHI) into consumer, personal, or unauthorized AI tools. Stanford AI Playground is approved for High-Risk non-PHI data; PHI review is in progress. PHI is permissible only within Stanford enterprise services explicitly approved for PHI under university Data Risk Assessment (DRA) and Business Associate Agreement (BAA) safeguards, currently including Stanford-managed ChatGPT Edu and Gemini Enterprise when logged in via Single Sign On with a Stanford-provided account. Claude for Education is approved for High Risk non-PHI data only; PHI processing is not covered. Institutional data approval does not grant clinical or coursework permission.

evidence.quote: To ensure that patient confidentiality is maintained at all times, no confidential research, patient data, or other protected health information (PHI) is to be entered into public AI platforms (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, OpenEvidence, Doximity, etc.).

evidence.quote: High-Risk non-PHI only; PHI review in progress for AI Playground.
evidence.location: Captured official text line 225; HTML text extraction; raw source retained privately

evidence.quote: Only approved for use with Stanford data when using a Stanford provided account through the UIT managed ChatGPT Edu service and logged in via Single Sign On.

clm-stanford-university-pwr-genai-policy.text: Stanford's Program in Writing and Rhetoric (PWR) prohibits students from using generative AI or LLMs to compose drafts or revisions for any major assignment in PWR courses, including composing or revising portions of essays or scripts, including paraphrases of LLM-generated writing. Students may not rely on generative AI summaries of sources. Violation of PWR's AI policy is treated as an Honor Code violation and results in involvement of the Office of Community Standards.

evidence.quote: Students may not use generative AI or LLMs to compose the drafts or revisions for any of the major assignments in their PWR classes. This includes using generative AI to compose or revise portions of their essay or scripts (from individual phrases or sentences to longer passages) or including in their essays/scripts paraphrases of LLM-generated writing or paraphrases of source material generated by LLMs. In addition, students may not rely on generative AI summaries of sources for their research and instead must actively read and engage themselves with the sources they draw on for their research projects and that they incorporate into their writing.

clm-harvard-university-social-studies-de.text: Social Studies prohibits generative or agentic AI assistance in submitted coursework, exams/quizzes and all thesis stages by default. Instructors may publish alternative syllabus rules but must require disclosure. Thesis exceptions are case-specific: obtain supervisor approval, submit the AI Policy Attestation request, and secure DUS approval by November 1 of senior year, or April 1 for off-cycle fall seniors. The AI Policy Attestation form is required in consultation with the supervisor at Prospectus submission and again in senior year. Thesis work cannot reuse AI-assisted work from another course merely because that course allowed it. These rules apply to Social Studies requirements.

topicBasis.privacy_data: Educational and research data rules apply in their own contexts. Staff administrative guidance explicitly excludes student learning, assessment and research. Examiners may not upload student work to GenAI.

topicBasis.research_publication: RDM framework version 4 requires research data and AI-use considerations across the research community. Its statement that there is no distinct GenAI research policy does not establish unrestricted use.
topicBasis.academic_integrity: Academic integrity and detector guidance have specific scopes. General discipline/appeal procedures remain unreviewed.
topicBasis.teaching_guidance: Faculty/course communication and student-work consent constraints apply in the stated contexts.
topicBasis.security_procurement: Review, procurement and risk assessment depend on the actual task, unit and data classification; staff administration is not student assessment.

scope.en: Read each cited rule for its course, academic unit, activity and exceptions. Site advice does not create a university obligation.

coursework.en: ETH Zurich advocates a proactive and responsible approach to generative AI in coursework. Students remain fully responsible for the content of any work they submit. Generative AI may serve a supplementary role (such as brainstorming, structuring, or coding assistance), but must never replace personal effort. Lecturers hold authority to determine whether and how generative AI may be used in their courses.
coursework.zh: AI 只能辅助，不能替代个人工作；学生对提交内容负责，教师决定课程及考核中的使用方式。

exams.en: Performance assessments must be conducted independently and personally by the student. The use of unauthorized aids, including generative AI tools not permitted by the examiner, constitutes academic misconduct subject to disciplinary action under the ETH Zurich Ordinance on Disciplinary Measures.

disclosure.en: ETH Zurich's declaration of originality provides two options: confirming that no generative AI was used, or confirming that authorised generative AI was used and its disclosure agreed with the supervisor. Bachelor's and Master's theses require a signed declaration of originality, while requirements for other written assessments depend on the applicable academic instructions. Doctoral candidates declare independent authorship through the doctoral examination registration process. The permitted use, disclosure format and any exceptions must follow the relevant supervisor and unit requirements. ETH Zurich's teaching guidelines instruct students to be transparent about their use of generative AI and to identify which tools contributed to which parts of their work, in accordance with applicable lecturer instructions and citation conventions. For scientific writing and theses, students should agree in advance with their supervisors on authorised AI use and disclosure requirements. ETH Library guidance recognises an exception where a supervisor has expressly agreed that particular AI use need not be separately declared. In the absence of such an agreement, undeclared use may constitute a breach of academic integrity.

Google AI tools have not yet been assessed by the CISO (assessment OPEN) and are not released for ETH confidential, strictly confidential, or protected personal data. Copyright and privacy must be respected at all times.

approved_tools.en: ETH Zurich recommends Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini, and Google NotebookLM for teaching purposes. research_publication.en: Researchers and students are fully responsible for the integrity of their scientific work and must verify AI-generated output, references, and facts. Generative AI tools cannot be listed as authors or cited as authoritative sources. Theses require signed originality declarations; doctoral candidates declare independent authorship upon registration for the doctoral examination. Researchers must comply with applicable funder (e.g. SNSF) and publisher guidelines.

academic_integrity.en: ETH Library provides Turnitin Originality to eligible professors and lecturers for text-similarity checking, subject to data classification and responsible selective-use guidance. Only public or internal documents may be uploaded. Similarity screening is distinct from AI-authorship detection; ETH Zurich warns that technical detection of AI-generated output is unreliable and should not be treated as conclusive evidence. Violations of GenAI guidelines such as use of unauthorised aids or non-disclosure of their use are subject to disciplinary action under existing performance assessment rules and the declaration of originality.

clm-ucl-genai-acknowledgement-and-refere.text: UCL Library guidance requires acknowledgement where GenAI has functionally contributed to the creation of academic work (e.g. drafting, planning, structuring), subject to discipline and assessment instructions. Minimum acknowledgement includes tool name and version, publisher, URL, and single-sentence context of use. Prompts, generation dates, and tracked-changes are additional requirements that apply only when stipulated by departments or assignment briefs. Preparatory reading, search summaries, and basic grammar assistance may not require acknowledgement. While UCL advises treating AI output as a work with no author, students and researchers must follow required departmental guidelines and standardised referencing styles (such as APA or Chicago), which may require citing the GenAI tool as an author.

clm-ucl-press-journals-editorial-policy-.text: UCL Press journals prohibit listing AI as an author on research-based works. Broadly, AI use in creating, editing, or manipulating images or figures is not accepted; however, an explicit exception permits AI-assisted technologies used as part of research design or methodology (e.g. data visualisation to generate or interpret underlying data), provided it is fully declared and documented in the methodology. Editors and peer reviewers are strictly prohibited from submitting manuscripts or data reported in them through AI tools.

clm-hku-assessment-instructor-instructio.text: HKU TALIC guidance requires teachers to clearly communicate acceptable AI use for course activities and assessed assignments. Instructors decide how to integrate AI; institutional tool access does not determine permission for a particular assessment.

evidence.quote: Teachers must be very clear in their guidance to students as to what is acceptable use of AI within the activities of their course and specifically on their assignments intended for assessment.
evidence.location: Transparency; public teaching guidance; normalized_extracted_text; quote characters 6696–6889; part 1/1.

clm-hku-law-ai-misuse-responses.text: For HKU Faculty of Law assessed work, an educative response may involve rewriting and resubmission with a penalty. Where this is not appropriate, an academic response may reduce the mark or give zero. Misuse may also be referred as a disciplinary offence; this is not automatic expulsion.

evidence.quote: When a teacher is satisfied that submitted work contains plagiarism or involves the misuse of generative and other AI tools, and that an educative response (usually involving re-writing and re-submission with a penalty) is not appropriate, then an academic response will be adopted, pursuant to which the plagiarized work may be given a mark of zero or a reduced mark. In addition, the matter may be treated as a disciplinary offence (just like the case of cheating during an examination) and referred to the University’s Disciplinary Committee under Statute XXXI of the University’s Statutes and the Disciplinary Committee Regulations.
evidence.location: Academic and disciplinary responses; normalized_extracted_text; quote characters 2805–3441; part 1/1.

clm-hku-law-permitted-ai-declaration.text: HKU Faculty of Law requires students to declare AI use on its assignment cover sheet where a teacher permits it for an assignment; failure to declare is treated as academic misconduct akin to plagiarism.

evidence.quote: In addition, the Faculty’s assignment cover sheet requires students to declare their use of AI tools, where this is permitted by a teacher for the purposes of an assignment. Failure to do so constitutes academic misconduct akin to plagiarism, and will be treated in the same manner.
evidence.location: Plagiarism and the Misuse of Generative and other AI tools in assessment; normalized_extracted_text; quote characters 2522–2804; part 1/1.

clm-hku-research-code-verification.text: HKU permits GenAI-generated research code only with documented and acknowledged use, verification of algorithms and software, and adequate testing that is conducted and reported.

evidence.quote: 23. Use of GenAI to generate computer code for research is only acceptable if a. the specific usage of the GenAI system is duly documented and acknowledged; b. the researcher has verified the correctness of the algorithm and software with respect to the intended use of the researcher; and c. the researcher conducts and reports adequate testing to ensure the software’s behaviours are well within user expectation.
evidence.location: Physical PDF page 4; section 23; dated 8 September 2025, Senate approval 23 September 2025.; raw_pdf_bytes; quote characters 10615–11030; part 1/1.

clm-hku-research-images-integrity.text: GenAI enhancement of research figures containing primary data is acceptable only if it does not alter interpretation. AI-generated images or other data should not be misrepresented as experimental data.

evidence.quote: 30. Use of GenAI tools to support image enhancement of figures that contain primary data is only acceptable if such modifications do not alter the interpretation of the data. 31. No AI-generated images and other data should be mis-represented as experimental data. F. Use of GenAI tools for peer reviewing research papers or funding applications
evidence.location: Physical PDF page 5; section 30–31; dated 8 September 2025, Senate approval 23 September 2025.; raw_pdf_bytes; quote characters 14332–14677; part 1/1.

clm-hku-research-peer-review-restriction.text: HKU does not accept use of GenAI in peer review of research outputs or funding applications because of integrity and confidentiality concerns.

evidence.quote: 32. The use of cloud-based commercial AI platforms has the potential to inadvertently disclose the content of papers or funding applications under review, thus violating the integrity and confidentiality of the established double-blind peer review process. Therefore, the use of GenAI in peer review of research output and funding applications is not acceptable.
evidence.location: Physical PDF page 5; section 32; dated 8 September 2025, Senate approval 23 September 2025.; raw_pdf_bytes; quote characters 14678–15040; part 1/1.

clm-ntu-ai-disclosure-submissions.text: NTU Library instructs students to disclose AI-tool use in their submissions and follow their module’s AI-use policy and instructor guidance. The required level of documentation and disclosure format depend on the assignment and instructor’s expectations; detailed prompt-and-output records and a particular declaration form are not universal requirements.

evidence.quote: Use AI tools to support tasks such as brainstorming, outlining, or checking grammar, but ensure you disclose their use in your submissions. Always refer to your module's AI use policy and seek guidance from your instructor regarding specific expectations for acceptable AI usage in your courses.
evidence.location: Key Points on Ethical AI Usage; normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 2828:3123

evidence.quote: When using AI for assignments (e.g., grammar checks, copyediting, or idea generation), adhere to the specific guidelines set by your instructor, as expectations may vary by module and discipline. This may include documenting your AI use, completing a “ Declaration on GAI Use ,” or disclosing AI contributions where required. To uphold academic integrity, you must always provide proper citations for all sources used, including AI‑generated content.
evidence.location: Purpose of Documenting, Disclosing and Citing AI Usage; normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 674:1124

clm-ntu-exam-external-resources-restrict.text: NTU Library instructs students not to access AI tools during examinations when external resources are not permitted. This condition does not establish either a ban in every exam or automatic AI permission in open-resource exams.

evidence.quote: Follow Exam Protocols. Do not access AI tools during examinations when external resources are not permitted to maintain fair testing conditions.
evidence.location: Consult, Follow Exam Protocols; normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 722:866

clm-ntu-extensive-ai-instructor-permissi.text: NTU Library instructs students to obtain explicit instructor permission for more extensive AI involvement, such as generating source materials or enhancing visuals.

evidence.quote: Obtain explicit permission from your instructor for more extensive AI involvement, such as generating source materials or enhancing visuals.
evidence.location: Key Points on Ethical AI Usage; normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 3124:3264

clm-ntu-genai-data-privacy.text: In research, confidential or sensitive information and personal data must not be uploaded to external GenAI platforms unless all applicable conditions are met: compliance with relevant laws and institutional policies; access restricted to authorised study members; no retention of the data in or by the GenAI; and, where applicable, explicit written permission from the data owner or agreement to that GenAI use in the Research Collaboration Agreement.

evidence.quote: Any confidential or sensitive information, and/or personal data must not be uploaded to any external GenAI software, system, or platform unless: The activity does not contravene any applicable laws, regulations, or institutional policies; Access to the GenAI is controlled and restricted to only authorised study members involved in the research; The data is not retained in or by the GenAI; and Where applicable, written permission has been explicitly provided by the data owner, or the use of such GenAI has been agreed upon in the Research Collaboration Agreement (RCA).
evidence.location: §4 Data Privacy & Confidentiality; normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 6791:7364

clm-ntu-research-experimental-images.text: AI-generated research visuals must not be presented as actual experimental data unless AI or AI-assisted tools are an essential component of the research design and/or methodology. Using AI to fabricate images resembling experimental results constitutes serious research misconduct.

evidence.quote: AI-generated images, figures and videos must not be presented as actual experimental data unless AI (or AI-assisted) tools are an essential component of the research design and/or methodology. The use of AI to fabricate images to resemble experimental results constitutes serious research misconduct.
evidence.location: §3(ii); normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 5691:5991

clm-ntu-research-misconduct-referral.text: The Vice President (Research) reviews the RIO preliminary report and may take appropriate action, decide whether to invite the Provost to appoint a COI for faculty/research staff, or decide whether to refer a student to the Board of Discipline. This is a research-misconduct process, not an automatic AI penalty or a finding of guilt.

evidence.quote: 4.4.1 The Vice President (Research) shall review the preliminary investigation report from the RIO, who will then take appropriate action (especially in relation to research staff), or decide whether to invite the Provost to appoint a COI to consider the Allegation/ Complaint under the Framework for Investigation and Disciplinary Proceedings for Faculty and Research Staff, or if the Respondent is a student, decide whether to refer to the Board of Discipline, or take any other appropriate action.

clm-uchicago-area-administrative-resolut.text: Under the general Area process, where a student acknowledges responsibility and warning/probation is the likely outcome, the Dean may offer administrative resolution. This is not an automatic AI penalty.

In such matters, the area Dean of Students can propose the sanction of an official warning or place the student on disciplinary probation for a specified period of time (e.g., a quarter, a year, for the duration of the student’s enrollment, etc.). clm-uchicago-law-submitted-work-default.text: Under the Law School default, AI use in submitted work is compared to unattributed use of a human author’s work. Some uses such as brainstorming or proofreading can comply; AI composing all or part of a paper violates the default even with attribution.

evidence.quote: b) For all work that a student submits for any form of academic credit, AI may not be used, whether with or without attribution, in a way that would constitute academic plagiarism if the AI were a human author whose work was used without attribution . Commentary: The crux of this policy, which applies in any context in which a student submits work for evaluation, is the application of existing academic integrity policies. Thus, some but not all uses of AI in preparing work to submit for a class would violate this default policy. Using AI to brainstorm ideas for a paper—akin to asking a search engine (like Google), professors, or professional contacts for
evidence.location: Law §4.9(1)(b); normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 7818:8480

evidence.quote: suggestions—would not violate this default policy. Nor would using AI for proofreading. The principle here is that if AI is performing a task that other technologies (or people) currently perform, and such uses are not a violation of academic integrity, then those uses of AI do not violate the default policy. In contrast, using AI to compose part or all of a paper, or copying or paraphrasing output from AI and passing it off as one’s own writing, would violate this default policy. The same principle applies here: if AI is performing a task that other technologies (or people) currently perform, and such uses are a violation of academic integrity, then those uses of AI do
evidence.location: Law §4.9(1)(b); normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 8481:9159

evidence.quote: violate the default policy. The default policy sweeps more broadly than a prohibition against academic plagiarism, however. A student cannot avoid limits on the use of AI that would otherwise apply by attributing their work to AI. It is not plagiarism to copy or paraphrase another’s work, so long as one properly cites that source. But under the default policy, the use of AI with or without attribution is compared to the use of a human-created source without attribution . Thus, using AI to compose all or part of a paper, even if the use of generative AI is fully documented in properly placed footnotes , is a violation of the default policy.
evidence.location: Law §4.9(1)(b); normalized extracted text; Unicode codepoints 9160:9807

topicBasis.coursework: No university-wide AI coursework permission, prohibition or mandate was established. Institutional tool access and comparative policy classifications cannot supply that missing assessment rule.
topicBasis.exams: Undergraduate examinations restrict devices unless the chief examiner provides otherwise and require independent answers. These are general exam rules, not a verified uniform AI examination policy for every student.
topicBasis.disclosure: Declarations are required in the specified School of Integrated Circuits doctoral proposal and comprehensive-examination documents. No universal PKU AI declaration requirement is established; pre-defense wording and the revision chain retain explicit gaps.
topicBasis.privacy_data: Administrative-data systems have scoped security obligations; China Economic Quarterly referees must not upload confidential review material to public AI. These do not impose a uniform student AI registration procedure.
topicBasis.approved_tools: The official directory lists 33 distinct services/resources. Access for Wenxue, Xiaobei and the teacher-facing Doujiao announcement has specific conditions; other directory entries do not establish universal accounts or assessment permission.
topicBasis.research_publication: Explicit restrictions apply to named School of Integrated Circuits doctoral procedures and China Economic Quarterly referees. The Department of Information Management comparative resource is not treated as binding university-wide policy.
